chunks: With this chain of transmission, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from al-Naḍr, from Ibn Sinān, who said:

I heard Abā ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام saying: “If a man does not find purifying means and he is in a state of janābah, then let him wipe from the earth and perform salat (prayer). Then when he finds water, let him perform ghusl, and the salat (prayer) that he performed has sufficed him.”

He said, may Allah the Exalted support him: If he caused himself to become junub deliberately, ghusl becomes obligatory upon him; and if he fears harm from it for himself, tayammum does not suffice him.

(573) 47. That is indicated by what al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me of, from Abī al-Qāsim Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, raising it, who said:
“If he caused himself to become junub, then he must perform ghusl according to whatever state he is in; but if he had a wet dream, he performs tayammum.”

key_terms.التَّيَمُّمُ: dry ablution performed with earth when water is unavailable
key_terms.الْأَرْضِ: the earth, from which tayammum is performed
key_terms.الْغُسْلُ: ritual bath required for major impurity
key_terms.جُنُبًا: being in a state of major ritual impurity requiring ghusl
key_terms.صَلَاتُهُ: his salat (prayer) performed in that state
key_terms.طَهُورًا: means of purification, especially purifying water or what serves in its place

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a junub person who cannot find water, and does tayammum suffice?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses the ruling of tayammum for a person in the state of janābah when water is unavailable. It also distinguishes between one who became junub deliberately and one who experienced ihtilām, indicating differing legal consequences in relation to ghusl and tayammum.
